Th e rhythmic sound of the waves crashing along the exposed coral that criss-crosses along the expanse of the coast greets the Traveler with a sense of 
serene peace as they approach the shores of Sol’Kesh. As the moon lowers over the brightening horizon, spiraling mounds of coral slowly reveal iridescent 
buds, expanding into dancing fronds of tendrils that bloom gold to meet the day, their gametes releasing and floating in the wind like motes of gentle 
dawn light. Down the coast, pillars of coral release theirs in kind, like a river in the sky, the gametes flow above the waves in a golden stream of life.
Th is fleeting moment of nature’s beauty is interrupted by the sound of chitinous skittering and the taint of rot spoiling the salt laden wind. Scuttling in 
their thousands, tiny ravenous crustaceans crawl over to the decaying daughon, as its being pulled ashore by three chittering illithisks with their hooked 
forelimbs.
Interested in documenting the new exciting life, the Traveler steps closer to witness, only for the clawed scavengers to all fall eerily still at once. In a single 
moment of unnerving silence, their black, stalked eyes swivel in unison to the lone intruder. Discarding the rotting mammal, they claw forward for the 
promise of a much fresher meal. Alarmed, the Traveler quickly steps back and looks for a means for defense. Spying a red stalk of coral strand, half sunk 
into the sand, they quickly grasp the staff of bone-like coral and prepares to ward off the incoming chitinous horde. 
Adapting to change is the only means for survival, and in no place else has this been more true than the coast. As the tide rises and falls with 
the steady passing of the moon above, as waters recede over eons of changing global temperatures, life has adapted to this intertidal zone 
unlike any other. With coral reefs transforming whole stretches of the ocean floor, spreading their colorful sanctuary for miles, the build 
up of their bones for generations pushed some species up past the waves to fi nd purchase. Th ese pioneers, like skyscrapers from a bygone 
age of ruin, stretched into the salt sprayed air. Th ey became home to countless winged creatures, as saturated with life as below, and soon 
colonized the land, weaving great strands of coral to both support and encroach on the sandy beaches and cliffs they now claim as their own.
In a biome entirely governed by the tide, much is revealed when it recedes, revealing wide strands of coral, pools of briny water 
teaming with life, and the voracious scavengers that rush across the newly exposed beach to pluck at the trapped creatures before 
the tide returns. More so than the biomes inland, the strands are rife with opportunity. No other creatures embody this than 
the cerrophol, gharril, and illithisk. Th ese rather devious creatures take great advantage of their amphibious nature, of their 
environment and strike out to snag prey whenever they have the chance. Cerrophol, adapting to life outside the water for short 
periods of time, climb into isolated tidal pools and devastate the cornered prey easily. Gharril feast on the beached remains of 
large fi sh and mammals, accumulating an ossifi ed pearl within their maw to spit out in a lethal barrage if disturbed from their 
meal. And the illithisk, with its scything arms folded in a nearly apologetic manner, lashes out at terrestrial prey, dragging them 
into the salty depths to drown. Although the predators and scavengers have made this mercurial biome dangerous, at night when 
the corals bloom to release their free floating gametes to sparkle on the moonlit air, it is truly something beautiful to witness. 
Ocean-borne winds break across the high cliffs that blow outwards onto ever smaller outcrops of land. Th ese shattered pieces of stone 
are far from lonely islands as coral bridge across them in web-like growths. Terrestrial corals creep up from the tidal line in ever-
vibrant displays of color and life, teeming with crustaceans and darting fi sh that weave around the coral strands and glowing white 
tentacles of eloom beneath the waves. As the sun rises to its zenith, a riotous pod of daugon can be heard over the crashing waves. 
Pulling their heavy, streamlined bodies onto the overlapping strands they lay out in the sun peacefully, their eyes closed and dorsal sails 
raised to soak in the heat before attempting another deep dive, thousands of feet beneath the sunlit surface to hunt for their favorite 
squid. Excited caws herald descending black beaked fi ngulls that eagerly pick off any sand mites from the resting mammals, their loud 
chattering alerting a nearby cerrophol that it may get an opportunity to snatch an unwary pup.
Traveling Along the Strands
Along stretches of coral that bridge islands, countless creatures 
live on and under the surface. Th ese strands harbor a dense 
ecosystem that, to an unwary Traveler, can spell disaster. As many 
of the corals that inhabit the Strands react differently when out 
of the water, some even resorting to carnivorous behavior when 
they can’t rely on a languid fi lter feeding existence. Th ough 
treacherous, even to walk along safely, there are unique resources 
that can be found on the strandsfor an adventurous sort: living 
plates of easily carved coral, dozens of venomous and stinging 
creatures to be harvested, and hundreds of unique species that 
make a home in this mercurial landscape.
Th e Strands are named for the long bridges of coral that weave 
in on themselves to rise above the waves and encroach on the 
shore. Traversing this type of living landscape is diffi cult as the 
criss-crossing pillars are festooned with symbiotic growths, both 
gnarly and easy to grip, as well as slippery slime molds that can 
easily cause a misstep.
To safely explore this environment, a Traveler must shift their 
perspective into seeing this land as not split between land and 
sea, but as one. Life has evolved to take advantage of the shifting 
tide, predators become prey as waters recede, pulling aquatic 
creatures into the suffocating air and vice versa. And so someone 
foreign to this quickly changing relationship must be ready to 
swim and climb when necessary, to know when a plant or coral 
is ready to be harvested, and when it is harvesting in kind.
